Get started with pkginspectr

Source: vignettes/pkginspectr.Rmd
pkginspectr.Rmd

pkginspectr answers simple questions about R packages: how many files, tests and help pages does a package have, and how many of its lines are code, comments or documentation? It works on local folders, GitHub repositories and CRAN packages, returns tidy tibbles, and draws bar charts right in the console.

library(pkginspectr)

A package to play with

pkginspectr ships a tiny example package so you can try everything offline. pkginspectr_example() returns its path:

example <- pkginspectr_example()

Every function below takes a path. It can be:

  • a local folder, such as "." for the package you are working on,
  • a GitHub repository, such as "r-lib/cli", or
  • the name of a CRAN package, such as "desc".

Remote packages can be pinned to a version, and prefixes make the source explicit:

path Meaning
"r-lib/cli@v3.6.0" GitHub tag, branch or commit
"github::apache/arrow/r" A package in a subfolder of a repository
"cran::desc@1.4.0" An older CRAN release
"local::pkgs/mypkg" A local folder, never looked up online

GitHub and CRAN packages are downloaded once and cached for the rest of the R session. With cache = "persistent", fixed versions (CRAN releases, GitHub tags and commits) are kept across sessions too. pkg_cache_clear() empties the cache.

Files and folders: pkg_structure() 

pkg_structure(example)
#> Inspecting examplepkg...
#> # pkginspectr: Package structure, 1 package
#> # A tibble:    1 × 11
#>   package    version num_files num_dirs num_r_files num_function_r_files
#>   <chr>      <chr>       <int>    <int>       <int>                <int>
#> 1 examplepkg 1.2.3           9        6           2                    1
#> # ℹ 5 more variables: num_non_function_r_files <int>, num_test_files <int>,
#> #   num_vignettes <int>, num_docs <int>, num_data_files <int>

num_r_files counts the scripts in R/, split into files that define at least one function and files that do not. num_test_files counts R files under tests/.

Lines of code: pkg_lines() 

lines <- pkg_lines(example)
#> Counting lines in examplepkg...
lines
#> # pkginspectr: Lines of code, 1 package
#> # A tibble:    1 × 11
#>   package version total_lines code_lines comment_lines roxygen_lines blank_lines
#>   <chr>   <chr>         <int>      <int>         <int>         <int>       <int>
#> 1 exampl… 1.2.3            32         21             2             4           5
#> # ℹ 4 more variables: r_lines <int>, test_lines <int>, other_lines <int>,
#> #   function_lines <int>

The columns break total_lines down in two ways, and each adds up to the total:

  • by type: code_lines, comment_lines, roxygen_lines and blank_lines;
  • by location: r_lines (in R/), test_lines (in tests/) and other_lines (e.g. data-raw/).
with(lines, code_lines + comment_lines + roxygen_lines + blank_lines)
#> [1] 32
with(lines, r_lines + test_lines + other_lines)
#> [1] 32

function_lines counts the code lines inside function definitions, so it is part of code_lines.

Lines are classified with R’s own parser rather than pattern matching. A # inside a string is not a comment, a { inside a string does not open a block, and functions are found however they are written: with <-, with =, as \(x) lambdas, or as anonymous functions passed to other calls.

Everything at once: pkg_summary()

pkg_summary() combines both tables. For GitHub or CRAN packages it downloads each package only once, so it is the quickest way to get everything:

pkg_summary(example)
#> Summarising examplepkg...
#> # pkginspectr: Package summary, 1 package
#> # A tibble:    1 × 20
#>   package    version num_files num_dirs num_r_files num_function_r_files
#>   <chr>      <chr>       <int>    <int>       <int>                <int>
#> 1 examplepkg 1.2.3           9        6           2                    1
#> # ℹ 14 more variables: num_non_function_r_files <int>, num_test_files <int>,
#> #   num_vignettes <int>, num_docs <int>, num_data_files <int>,
#> #   total_lines <int>, code_lines <int>, comment_lines <int>,
#> #   roxygen_lines <int>, blank_lines <int>, r_lines <int>, test_lines <int>,
#> #   other_lines <int>, function_lines <int>

Individual functions: pkg_functions()

pkg_functions() goes one level deeper and returns one row per named function, with its size, number of arguments and whether the package exports it:

fns <- pkg_functions(example)
#> Listing functions in examplepkg...
fns
#> # pkginspectr: Functions, 3 functions in 1 package
#> # A tibble:    3 × 9
#>   package    version file     location name     line code_lines n_args exported
#>   <chr>      <chr>   <chr>    <chr>    <chr>   <int>      <int>  <int> <lgl>   
#> 1 examplepkg 1.2.3   R/funs.R R        add_one     5          3      1 TRUE    
#> 2 examplepkg 1.2.3   R/funs.R R        square     10          1      1 FALSE   
#> 3 examplepkg 1.2.3   R/funs.R R        compose    12          3      2 FALSE

That makes questions such as “which functions are longest?” or “how much of the package is internal?” one-liners:

fns[order(fns$code_lines, decreasing = TRUE), c("name", "code_lines")]
#> Warning: Unknown or uninitialised column: `package`.
#> # pkginspectr: Functions, 3 functions in 0 packages
#> # A tibble:    3 × 2
#>   name    code_lines
#>   <chr>        <int>
#> 1 add_one          3
#> 2 compose          3
#> 3 square           1
table(exported = fns$exported)
#> exported
#> FALSE  TRUE 
#>     2     1

Following a package over time

pkg_versions() lists every CRAN release of a package with its date, and pkg_history() runs pkg_summary() on several of them. By default it picks five releases spread across the package’s history, always including the first and the latest:

pkg_versions("dplyr")

history <- pkg_history("dplyr")
history |>
  dplyr::select(package, version, date, num_r_files, code_lines)

Plot it with type = "metric" to see each metric grow release by release. Rows are labelled with their version:

pkg_plot(history, type = "metric")

Use versions to pick releases yourself, and cache = "persistent" to keep them for next time, since old releases never change:

pkg_history("dplyr", versions = c("0.8.0", "1.0.0", "1.1.0"), cache = "persistent")

Derived metrics

pkginspectr returns raw counts on purpose: they are unambiguous and add up. Ratios are often more useful, especially when comparing packages of very different sizes, and each is a single line of dplyr. Copy the ones you need.

library(dplyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE)

summary <- pkg_summary(example, quiet = TRUE)

Package-level ratios 

summary |>
  transmute(
    package,
    # Lines in tests/ for every line in R/
    test_to_code = test_lines / r_lines,
    # Share of all lines that are comments or roxygen documentation
    comment_density = (comment_lines + roxygen_lines) / total_lines,
    # Share of code that sits inside function definitions
    function_share = function_lines / code_lines,
    # Average size of a script in R/
    lines_per_r_file = r_lines / num_r_files
  )
#> # pkginspectr: Package statistics, 1 package
#> # A tibble:    1 × 5
#>   package    test_to_code comment_density function_share lines_per_r_file
#>   <chr>             <dbl>           <dbl>          <dbl>            <dbl>
#> 1 examplepkg         0.28           0.188          0.333             12.5

r_lines includes the roxygen comments in R/, so test_to_code is a conservative measure: heavily documented packages score a little lower.

Function-level summaries

pkg_functions() lends itself to per-package summaries of function size and API surface:

functions <- pkg_functions(example, quiet = TRUE) |>
  filter(location == "R") |>
  group_by(package) |>
  summarise(
    n_functions = n(),
    n_exported = sum(exported, na.rm = TRUE),
    share_internal = mean(!exported, na.rm = TRUE),
    median_lines = median(code_lines),
    longest = max(code_lines),
    .groups = "drop"
  )
functions
#> # A tibble: 1 × 6
#>   package    n_functions n_exported share_internal median_lines longest
#>   <chr>            <int>      <int>          <dbl>        <int>   <int>
#> 1 examplepkg           3          1          0.667            3       3

Combining tables

Joining the two gives ratios that need both, such as help pages per exported function. num_docs counts every .Rd file, including package-level and internal topics, so treat it as a rough indicator:

summary |>
  select(package, num_docs) |>
  left_join(functions, by = "package") |>
  transmute(package, num_docs, n_exported, docs_per_export = num_docs / n_exported)
#> # pkginspectr: Package structure, 1 package
#> # A tibble:    1 × 4
#>   package    num_docs n_exported docs_per_export
#>   <chr>         <int>      <int>           <dbl>
#> 1 examplepkg        1          1               1

Plotting derived metrics

pkg_plot() works on any data frame with a package column, so derived metrics can be plotted too. Use type = "metric", which scales each metric on its own, because ratios on different scales do not belong on one bar chart:

pkg_summary(c("r-lib/cli", "r-lib/fs", "desc"), quiet = TRUE) |>
  transmute(
    package,
    test_to_code = test_lines / r_lines,
    comment_density = (comment_lines + roxygen_lines) / total_lines
  ) |>
  pkg_plot(type = "metric", title = "Testing and documentation")

What gets counted

pkginspectr counts the files that R CMD build would put into the package tarball. It skips version-control folders such as .git/, R’s standard exclusions such as .Rproj.user/ and .Rhistory, and anything listed in the package’s .Rbuildignore, which often includes docs/ and data-raw/.

This matters when comparing packages: a local checkout and the CRAN release of the same package give comparable numbers. To count .Rbuildignored files as well, use include_ignored = TRUE:

pkg_lines(".", include_ignored = TRUE)

Plotting in the console

pkg_plot(), or simply plot(), draws bar charts in the console. The default view shows one panel per package, with each metric as a share of its total:

plot(lines)
#> ── pkginspectr: Lines of code ──────────────────────────────────────────────────
#> 
#> ── examplepkg 1.2.3 ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#> Lines (share of total_lines)
#> total_lines     32  100.0%  ▏████████████████████████████████████████▕
#> code_lines      21   65.6%  ▏██████████████████████████▕
#> comment_lines    2    6.2%  ▏██▕
#> roxygen_lines    4   12.5%  ▏█████▕
#> blank_lines      5   15.6%  ▏██████▕
#> r_lines         25   78.1%  ▏███████████████████████████████▕
#> test_lines       7   21.9%  ▏█████████▕
#> other_lines      0    0.0%  ▏▕
#> function_lines   7   21.9%  ▏█████████▕

With several packages, type = "metric" shows one panel per metric instead, with bars scaled to the largest value:

pkg_summary(c("r-lib/cli", "r-lib/fs", "desc")) |>
  pkg_plot(type = "metric")

Bars are plain characters, so you can restyle them:

pkg_plot(
  lines,
  bar_col = "darkorange",
  glyph = "=",
  start = "[",
  end = "]",
  max_bars = 20,
  title = "examplepkg at a glance"
)
#> ── examplepkg at a glance ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#> 
#> ── examplepkg 1.2.3 ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#> Lines (share of total_lines)
#> total_lines     32  100.0%  [====================]
#> code_lines      21   65.6%  [=============]
#> comment_lines    2    6.2%  [=]
#> roxygen_lines    4   12.5%  [==]
#> blank_lines      5   15.6%  [===]
#> r_lines         25   78.1%  [================]
#> test_lines       7   21.9%  [====]
#> other_lines      0    0.0%  []
#> function_lines   7   21.9%  [====]

Quiet mode

All functions report progress as they go. Use quiet = TRUE to turn the messages off, for example in scripts or reports:

pkg_lines(example, quiet = TRUE)
#> # pkginspectr: Lines of code, 1 package
#> # A tibble:    1 × 11
#>   package version total_lines code_lines comment_lines roxygen_lines blank_lines
#>   <chr>   <chr>         <int>      <int>         <int>         <int>       <int>
#> 1 exampl… 1.2.3            32         21             2             4           5
#> # ℹ 4 more variables: r_lines <int>, test_lines <int>, other_lines <int>,
#> #   function_lines <int>
